cues.x: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, by Stephen R. Covey.
Let me begin with a story that Stephen Covey tells about himself, because it is the moment the whole book was born.
Covey and his wife were quietly worried about their son.
The boy was struggling in every way a boy can struggle.
He was doing poorly in school.
He was awkward and immature, so far behind the other children socially that it was painful to watch.
He was small for his age, uncoordinated, picked last for every team.

And Covey, who taught leadership and communication for a living, who literally lectured other people on how to build successful children, was pouring encouragement into this boy and getting nothing back.
He and his wife tried everything.
They cheered.
They coached.
They modeled a positive attitude.
They tried to build the boy up.
And the harder they tried, the more the boy seemed to shrink.
Then Covey noticed something uncomfortable about himself.
As he examined what he was actually doing, he realized that underneath all the encouragement, deep down, he did not really believe his son was okay.
He saw the boy as inadequate, as behind, as someone who needed to be fixed.
And no matter how many positive words came out of his mouth, the boy was receiving the true message underneath, which was, you are not enough as you are.
Covey and his wife made a decision that changed their family and eventually shaped this entire book.
They decided to stop trying to change the boy, and instead to change themselves.
Not their technique, but their actual seeing.
They worked to genuinely appreciate their son for who he was, to enjoy him, to stop comparing him, to release the anxiety that was leaking out of them.
And slowly, given room to breathe and be himself, the boy began to flourish.
He gained confidence at his own pace and eventually excelled, in academics, in sports, in relationships, far beyond what anyone had expected.
Covey draws a huge lesson from this small family drama, and it is the foundation of everything that follows.
The problem was never the boy.
The problem was the way Covey was seeing the boy.
He calls this a paradigm, which is just a fancy word for the mental map you carry around, the way you perceive and interpret the world.
And his central claim is that we do not see the world as it is.
We see the world as we are.
Our maps are not the territory.
And when our map is wrong, no amount of effort or positive attitude on top of that wrong map will fix things.
You can work harder, think more positively, and try new techniques all day long, but if you are working off a flawed map, you are just getting more efficiently lost.
Real change, the deep and lasting kind, does not come from changing your behavior on the surface.
It comes from changing the paradigm underneath, from seeing differently.
And that is why he calls this an inside-out approach.
You start on the inside, with your own character and your own way of seeing, and the outside follows.
To make this vivid, he tells another story, this one on a New York subway.
It is a quiet Sunday morning.
People are sitting peacefully, some reading, some resting with their eyes closed.
Then a man gets on with his children, and the children are wild.
They are yelling, throwing things, grabbing people's papers, completely out of control.
And the man just sits there next to Covey, eyes closed, doing nothing.
Covey feels irritation rising.
Everyone on the car is being disturbed by these children, and this father is oblivious, not lifting a finger.
Finally Covey, with what he thought was admirable patience, turns to the man and says, sir, your children are really disturbing a lot of people.
I wonder if you couldn't control them a little more.
The man lifts his gaze as if coming out of a fog and says softly, oh, you're right.
I guess I should do something about it.
We just came from the hospital where their mother died about an hour ago.
I don't know what to think, and I guess they don't know how to handle it either.
Covey says that in an instant, everything changed.
His irritation vanished.
His whole way of seeing the situation shifted.
He suddenly saw grieving children and a shattered father, and his heart filled with compassion.
Nothing about the situation had changed except the information, and yet his entire experience of it transformed.
That is a paradigm shift.
And Covey's point is that the effective life is largely a matter of getting your paradigms right, because everything you do flows out of how you see.
Covey used to demonstrate this in the classroom with an experiment I love, because it makes the abstract idea land in your body.
He would split a room of students in half.
He would hand one half a card with a drawing of a lovely young woman, elegant, wearing a feathered hat, her face turned away.
He would give them ten seconds to look at it, then take the card back.
Then he would hand the other half of the room a different card, a drawing of a haggard old woman with a huge hooked nose and a shawl, and give them ten seconds too.
Then he would put a third image up on the screen at the front of the room, the famous composite drawing that contains both women at once, depending on how you read the lines.
He would ask, what do you see?
And the room would split down the middle.
One half saw a beautiful young woman, obviously, unmistakably.
The other half saw an old crone, equally obviously.
And then they would begin to argue.
Not politely.
People would get genuinely heated, because each side could see with their own eyes what was plainly there, and the other side was clearly being stubborn or stupid.
It took real effort, real patience, for someone to say, all right, show me.
Where is her chin?
And the moment the other person walked them through the lines, the picture would flip, and there she was, the other woman, who had been on the page the entire time.
Covey's point is not a parlor trick.
Those students had been conditioned for ten seconds.
Ten seconds.
And that ten seconds was enough to make them absolutely certain, and to make them dismiss people who saw it differently.
Now consider that you have been conditioned for decades, by your family, your school, your religion, your culture, your successes and your wounds.
How certain should you be that the way you see your spouse, your colleague, your own possibilities, is simply the way it is?
This is why Covey says the way you see the problem is the problem, and why the person who can say show me, and mean it, has an enormous advantage in life.
Now, before he gives you a single habit, Covey makes a distinction that is really the spine of the whole book.
He says that in the early history of American success writing, roughly the first hundred and fifty years, the literature focused on what he calls the character ethic.
It taught that success flowed from things like integrity, humility, fidelity, courage, justice, patience, hard work, simplicity, and the Golden Rule.
Success was a matter of who you actually were, of your character, built slowly over time.
But then, Covey noticed, somewhere after the First World War, the writing shifted.
It moved toward what he calls the personality ethic.
Now success was framed as a function of personality, of public image, of attitudes and behaviors and techniques.
It became about surface things, about how to make people like you, how to project confidence, how to use influence tricks to get what you want.
It was quicker.
It was easier.
And it was, at its worst, a kind of manipulation, a set of shortcuts.
Covey does not say the personality ethic is entirely worthless.
Some of those skills matter.
But he warns that they are secondary, and that when we try to build a life on personality techniques while ignoring the character foundation underneath, we are building on sand.
You cannot fake your way to a good marriage with communication tricks if the underlying character is not there.
You cannot manipulate your way to lasting trust.
Sooner or later the technique fails and the real you shows through.
He puts it bluntly.
What you are shouts so loudly in my ears that I cannot hear what you say.
The 7 Habits, then, are not personality techniques.
They are a character-based, principle-centered approach.
They are about aligning yourself with timeless principles, the way a compass aligns with true north, so that you are not just doing effective things but genuinely becoming an effective person.
It is worth knowing where this distinction came from, because it is not an opinion Covey pulled out of the air.
For his doctoral work, he sat down and read essentially everything written about success in the United States since seventeen seventy six.
Two hundred years of it.
Self-help books, essays, sermons, business manuals, the whole sprawling library of American advice.
And as he read chronologically, he watched the shift happen in front of him.
The early material was almost entirely about character.
The later material, the stuff from the last fifty years or so, was overwhelmingly about image, technique, and quick fixes.
He calls the deep kind primary greatness, the greatness of who you actually are, and the surface kind secondary greatness, which is public recognition, talent, reputation.
Secondary greatness is real, and it is nice to have.
But if you chase it without the primary kind, the gap eventually shows, and the people closest to you feel it first.
Your colleagues might be fooled.
Your spouse and your children will not be.
He gives two images to nail this down, and both are worth carrying with you.
The first is the law of the farm.
In school, he says, you can cram.
You can goof off for a semester, then panic, pull three all-nighters, memorize enough to pass, and get a grade that looks like learning.
But try that on a farm.
Try forgetting to plant in the spring, ignoring the field all summer, and then working frantically in the autumn to force a harvest.
The farm is a natural system, and natural systems do not accept cramming.
You pay the price, in the right season, or you get nothing.
Character, relationships, health, and skill are all farms, not classrooms.
There are no shortcuts, and the people who try to take them are simply choosing to pay later, with interest.
The second image is a story Covey attributes to a naval training account, and he tells it because it is funny and unforgettable.
A battleship is out at night in heavy weather.
The lookout reports a light off the starboard bow, holding steady, on a collision course.
The captain signals across, change your course twenty degrees.
The reply comes back, advise you change your course twenty degrees.
The captain, irritated, signals, I am a captain, change course twenty degrees.
Reply: I am a seaman second class, advise you change course twenty degrees.
Now furious, the captain signals, I am a battleship, change course twenty degrees.
And back comes the answer: I am a lighthouse.
The captain changed course.
Principles, Covey says, are lighthouses.
They do not move for your rank, your cleverness, or your urgency.
You can argue with them all night, and you will still be the one who has to turn.
He organizes the seven habits along a path he calls the maturity continuum, and it moves through three stages.
We all begin life in dependence.
As infants and children, we depend completely on others.
The dependent person says you.
You take care of me, you are to blame, you did not come through.
From there, the goal our culture celebrates is independence.
The independent person says I.
I can do it, I am responsible, I am self-reliant.
And most success literature stops right there, treating independence as the summit.
But Covey says independence is not the highest stage.
There is one more, and it is the one mature relationships and great achievements actually require.
It is interdependence.
The interdependent person says we.
We can do it, we can combine our talents, we can create something together that neither of us could create alone.
The first three habits, he says, take you from dependence to independence.
They are private victories, won inside yourself, where nobody is watching.
The next three habits take you from independence to interdependence.
They are public victories, won in your relationships with others.
And the seventh habit surrounds and renews all of them.
So let me walk you through them, one at a time.
Habit one is be proactive.
This is the foundational habit, the one everything else stands on, and Covey means something deeper by it than just taking initiative.
He means recognizing that between what happens to you and how you respond, there is a gap, and in that gap lies your freedom to choose.
He builds this on the story of Viktor Frankl, the psychiatrist who survived the Nazi death camps.

Stripped of everything, his family killed, his body tortured, naked in a cell, Frankl discovered what he called the last of the human freedoms, the freedom to choose his own response to his circumstances.
His captors controlled everything about his environment, but they could not control what happened inside him unless he let them.
Covey takes that and says it is true for all of us, though our trials are usually far smaller.
We are not simply products of our conditioning, our genes, or our environment.
We are products of our choices.
Between stimulus and response, we get to choose.
He contrasts proactive people with reactive people.
Reactive people are driven by feelings, by circumstances, by conditions, by their environment.
When the weather is good, they feel good.
When people treat them well, they feel fine.
When people treat them poorly, they become defensive and miserable, because their emotional life is at the mercy of others' behavior.
Proactive people carry their own weather with them.
They are driven by values, carefully chosen and internalized values.
They can be acted upon by the outside, but their response is a product of their own conscious choice.
Listen to the language, Covey says, because it reveals the paradigm.
Reactive language sounds like, there's nothing I can do, that's just the way I am, he makes me so mad, I have to do that, I can't.
Proactive language sounds like, let's look at our alternatives, I can choose a different approach, I control my own feelings, I will choose an appropriate response.
The reactive person makes themselves a victim.
The proactive person keeps the power.
Covey loves the story of Anwar Sadat here, the Egyptian president.
Sadat had been raised, scripted really, in a deep hatred of Israel.
He had thundered publicly that he would never shake the hand of an Israeli as long as they occupied one inch of Arab land.
Never.
But as a young man, Sadat had spent time locked in cell fifty four of Cairo Central Prison, and in that cell he had learned something about the interior life.
He had learned that he could sit apart from his own mind and watch it, and that a person who cannot change the very fabric of his thought will never be able to change reality.

Years later, as president, facing an intractable situation, Sadat went back into that interior room, rewrote his own script, and then walked into the Israeli Knesset in Jerusalem and opened one of the most extraordinary peace initiatives of the century.
He changed a paradigm he had held his entire adult life.
And Covey's point is that if a man can rewrite a script that deep, under that much political pressure, then the scripts you and I are carrying around are hardly permanent either.
He also throws down a challenge, and it is the best homework in the book.
He calls it the thirty day test.
For thirty days, work only in your circle of influence.
Make small commitments and keep them.
Be a light, not a judge.
Be a model, not a critic.
Be part of the solution, not part of the problem.
Do not accuse, do not argue about other people's weaknesses, do not defend your own.
When you make a mistake, admit it, correct it, and learn from it without blaming.
Do not let a failure on the outside become a failure on the inside.
Thirty days of that, he says, and you will not simply feel better.
You will watch your influence physically expand, because people respond to a person who has stopped complaining and started producing.
He gives you a beautiful tool here, two circles.
Draw a big circle and call it the circle of concern.
Inside it goes everything you care about, the economy, the weather, your health, your children, the national debt, the behavior of your boss, the possibility of war, all of it.
Now draw a smaller circle inside that one and call it the circle of influence.
Inside the smaller circle goes only the things you can actually do something about.
Covey's insight is that you can tell a proactive person from a reactive one by where they put their energy.
Reactive people pour their energy into the circle of concern, into all the things they cannot control.
They obsess over other people's weaknesses, over problems in the environment, over circumstances beyond their reach.
And here is the tragedy.
All that negative energy, focused on things they cannot change, combined with the neglect of the things they can, actually causes their circle of influence to shrink.
Proactive people do the opposite.
They pour their energy into the circle of influence, into the things they can affect.
And that positive energy is expansive.
Their circle of influence grows.
The way to change your marriage is not to focus on your spouse's flaws, which sit in your circle of concern, but to work on yourself, which sits squarely in your circle of influence.
Work on the inner circle, and watch it enlarge.
Habit two is begin with the end in mind.
Covey opens this one by asking you to do something a little uncomfortable.
He asks you to picture your own funeral.
Imagine you are driving to a chapel, and you realize the funeral is yours, three years from now.
You walk in and see the flowers, hear the soft music, and there in the casket is you.
And there are four speakers.
One is a family member.
One is a friend.
One is someone from your work.
And one is from your church or community.
Now, Covey asks, what do you want each of those four people to say about you?
What kind of husband, wife, parent, child do you want their words to reflect?
What kind of friend, what kind of colleague?
Sit with that, he says, because your answers are your deepest values.
They are the end you actually want.
And most of us, he warns, have never clearly defined that end.
We climb the ladder of success only to discover, when we reach the top, that it was leaning against the wrong wall.
We can be busy, efficient, and productive, and still be climbing the wrong wall the entire time.
Beginning with the end in mind means that all things are created twice.
There is a mental creation first, and a physical creation second.
You do not build a house by grabbing a hammer.
You build it first in your mind, in blueprints, down to the last detail, and only then do you build it in bricks.
The same is true of a life.

If you do not consciously do the first creation, deciding what your life is for, then someone else, or your circumstances, or old scripts from your childhood, will do it for you by default, and you will live out a plan you never chose.

The great tool Covey offers here is a personal mission statement, a written declaration of what you want to be and to do, of the character and contributions and values that are the constitution of your life.
When you have that, you have a standard against which you can measure every decision.
It becomes your true north.
There is a distinction hiding inside this habit that is worth the whole chapter on its own, the difference between leadership and management.
Covey paints a picture.
Imagine a crew of workers hacking their way through a thick jungle with machetes.
They are the producers, cutting the undergrowth, clearing the path.

Behind them come the managers, sharpening the machetes, writing policy manuals, building muscle development programs, bringing in improved technologies and setting up working schedules and compensation plans for the machete wielders.
And then there is the leader, who climbs the tallest tree, surveys the entire situation, and yells down, wrong jungle.
And what do the busy, efficient producers and managers shout back?
Shut up, we are making progress.
Management, Covey says, is doing things right.
Leadership is doing the right things.
Management is efficiency in climbing the ladder.
Leadership determines whether the ladder is leaning against the right wall.
Both matter, but leadership comes first, and it is the one almost everyone skips, because climbing feels like progress and climbing the tree feels like stopping.
He deepens this with the idea of being principle-centered.
He points out that everyone has a center, something at the heart of their life from which everything else flows, and for most people that center is unstable.
Some people center their lives on their spouse, and become emotionally dependent and devastated by every marital ripple.
Some center on money, some on work, some on possessions, some on pleasure, some on friends or enemies, some on their church, some on themselves.
And every one of these centers, Covey says, is shaky, because it rises and falls with something outside your control.
The one stable center, the one that does not shift, is a center built on correct principles.
Principles like fairness, honesty, integrity, human dignity, service, growth.
These do not change.
They do not react.
They do not die or leave you or get taken away.
Build your life on them and you have an unshakeable core.
Habit three is put first things first.
This is where the private victory gets real, because this is the habit of execution, of living out what you decided in habits one and two.
Covey introduces his famous time management matrix, and I want you to really picture it, because it is the practical heart of the book.
Draw a square and divide it into four boxes.
Along the top, label the two columns urgent and not urgent.
Along the side, label the two rows important and not important.
Now every activity in your life falls into one of the four resulting boxes, and Covey names them quadrants one through four.
Quadrant one is both urgent and important.
These are the crises, the pressing problems, the deadline-driven projects.
The fire is burning, and you must deal with it.
Quadrant two is important but not urgent.
This is planning, prevention, relationship building, learning, exercise, preparation, the things that matter deeply but never scream at you.
Quadrant three is urgent but not important.
These are the interruptions, the ringing phones, the emails marked urgent that are really someone else's priority pressing in on you, the meetings that feel pressing but accomplish little.
Quadrant four is neither urgent nor important, the pure time-wasters, the mindless scrolling, the trivial busywork, the escape activities.
Here is Covey's crucial insight.
Most people spend their lives reacting to what is urgent, bouncing between quadrant one and quadrant three, driven by whatever is loudest.
They put out fires all day, and when they need relief they collapse into quadrant four.
But the secret of effective people, he says, is that they live in quadrant two.
They invest their time in the important-but-not-urgent activities, the ones that prevent the crises before they start.
If you exercise regularly, you prevent the health crisis.
If you maintain your relationships, you prevent the relationship crisis.
If you plan and prepare, you prevent the deadline emergency.
The more time you spend in quadrant two, the smaller quadrant one becomes, because you are handling things before they catch fire.
But quadrant two requires you to be proactive, because it never announces itself.
Nothing external will ever push you to do the important-but-not-urgent thing.
You have to say yes to it deliberately, which means you have to say no to a great many urgent but unimportant things.
And Covey says you can only say no with a peaceful heart when you have a bigger yes burning inside you, the yes of your mission and your deepest priorities.
Effective people are not primarily people who manage their time well.
They are people who manage themselves well, who have the integrity to act on what matters most even when it is not the thing shouting the loudest.
So how do you actually live in quadrant two?
Covey's answer is to stop organizing your life daily and start organizing it weekly, and to organize it around roles rather than tasks.
Here is the process.
Sit down once a week, on a Sunday evening perhaps, and first write down your roles.
Not your tasks, your roles.
You might be an individual, a spouse, a parent, a manager of this project, a friend, a member of a community, a son or daughter.
Six or seven of them is typical.
Then, for each role, ask what is the one or two most important things I could do in this role this week that would make the biggest difference.
Those are your goals, and most of them will be quadrant two goals, because that is where importance lives.
Only then do you open your calendar and schedule those things first, blocking real time for them, before the week fills up on its own.
And then, day by day, you adapt.
Notice the inversion.
Most people schedule their priorities.
Covey wants you to prioritize your schedule, which means the important things get their appointment before the urgent things arrive to claim it.
He calls this the fourth generation of time management, and its whole aim is not to cram more in but to make sure that the things that go in are the right things.
The other engine of quadrant two is delegation, and Covey draws a sharp line between two kinds.
There is gofer delegation, which is go for this, go for that, do this, then come back and I will tell you the next step.
You are the boss, the other person is a pair of hands, and you have to supervise every move, which means you have not really freed any of your own time.
And there is stewardship delegation, which focuses on results instead of methods.
It takes longer at the start and it pays forever.
Covey says a proper stewardship agreement has five parts, and they are worth memorizing.
One, desired results, a clear mutual understanding of what is to be accomplished, described vividly, with the what and the when but not the how.
Two, guidelines, the boundaries and the known failure paths, the places where you say, here is where people have historically fallen into quicksand.
Three, resources, the human, financial and organizational support available.
Four, accountability, the standard of performance and when you will report against it.
Five, consequences, what happens as a result, good and bad.
He illustrates it with a story from his own front lawn, and it is one of the most beloved passages in the book.
Covey decided to delegate the care of the yard to his seven year old son, Stephen.
He did not just hand him a hose.
He spent two weeks training him first.
He walked the boy around the neighborhood and said, look at that yard, see how green and clean it is.
Then look at ours.
Do you see the yellow spots?
Green and clean, that is the job.
He showed him that how the grass got green was up to him.
He could use the sprinklers or buckets or spit, Covey said, as long as it was green.
He showed him that clean meant no messes, and he made a point of picking up one gum wrapper himself while explaining.
He asked the boy who his boss would be.
You are, Dad.
No, Covey said.
You are.
You boss yourself.
I am your helper.
And they agreed to walk the yard together twice a week so the boy could report on his own work.
Then Covey did the hard part.
He waited.
For two weeks, nothing happened.
The yard turned yellow.
Trash accumulated.
Covey, watching from the window on a hot Saturday, was dying inside, because he had invested all this training and here was the boy playing while the lawn browned.
Finally, on the walk-around, the boy looked at the mess and his lip started to quiver and he began to cry.
It's so hard, Dad.
Covey says the temptation right then was enormous, either to snap and take the job back, or to rescue the boy and do it himself.
He did neither.
He said, is there anything I can do to help?
Because he had promised to be the helper.
And the boy asked, would you?
Covey went inside, got two sacks, and picked up the mess the boy pointed to, exactly what he was asked to do and nothing more.
From that moment, the boy owned the yard.
He kept it green and clean all summer, often to a higher standard than his father had.

The lesson Covey pulls out is that stewardship delegation costs you enormous patience in the short run and buys you enormous leverage in the long run, and that the moment you take the job back to relieve your own discomfort, you have taught the person that they are not really responsible after all.
With those three habits, you have moved from dependence to independence.
You have become a self-mastered person.
But now Covey turns to the public victories, and here he pauses to lay a foundation, because you cannot have healthy relationships without it.
He introduces the emotional bank account.
It works exactly like a financial account.
When you are kind, keep your promises, listen, show respect, and are loyal to people when they are absent, you make deposits.
Trust rises.
When you are unkind, break promises, betray confidences, and treat people with contempt, you make withdrawals.
Trust falls.
And when the account is overdrawn, when the trust is gone, communication becomes almost impossible.
You can say all the right words and they land wrong, because there is no trust to carry them.
He names six major deposits.
Understanding the other person, which is putting yourself in their shoes.
Attending to the little things, because in relationships the little things are the big things.
Keeping commitments.
Clarifying expectations up front, so you do not withdraw trust over a misunderstanding.
Showing personal integrity, especially loyalty to people who are not in the room.
And, when you make a withdrawal, sincerely apologizing.
The emotional bank account is the reservoir that all the public habits draw from.
Habit four is think win-win.
Covey says most of us are scripted from childhood in win-lose thinking.
School grades on a curve, so my A depends on your B. Sports produce a winner and a loser.
We learn to see life as a competition, a zero-sum game, where for me to win, you must lose.

There is also lose-win, the doormat who caves to keep the peace, and lose-lose, the vindictive spiral where two people are so bent on the other's defeat that they both go down together, and there is win, the person who just wants to get theirs and does not care what you get.
But Covey argues that in any interdependent relationship, the only frame that works over the long run is win-win.
Win-win is the belief that there is enough for everyone, that one person's success does not require another's failure, that we can find solutions that genuinely benefit us both.

It comes from what he calls an abundance mentality, the deep sense that there is plenty out there, as opposed to the scarcity mentality that sees life as a fixed pie where any slice you get is a slice taken from me.
And he adds a courageous fifth option.
If you cannot reach a genuine win-win, the mature choice is win-win or no deal.
If we cannot find a solution that is good for both of us, we agree to disagree agreeably and walk away, rather than forcing a deal in which one of us loses and resentment poisons the relationship.
That freedom to say no deal is what lets you hold out for a real win-win instead of settling.
He also insists that win-win is not just an attitude, it is a system, and this is where a lot of well-meaning organizations trip.
He describes a company president who called him in, frustrated, saying, our problem is that our people are selfish, they will not cooperate.
Covey asked to look around.

The man walked him into a room where there was a chart on the wall, and on the chart were racehorses, one for each salesman, and they were racing toward a picture of Bermuda, because the top seller would win a trip there with his wife.
So on Monday the president gave a speech about teamwork, and every other day of the week the system paid people to beat each other.
Covey's line for this is that companies routinely reward A while hoping for B.
If your compensation, your promotions and your recognition all reward win-lose, no amount of talk about cooperation will survive contact with the pay slip.

The fix, he says, requires five things working together: character, which is integrity, maturity and an abundance mentality; relationships built on trust; performance agreements that spell out the win for both sides; supportive systems that actually pay for the behavior you want; and processes that get there through empathy and synergy rather than through force.
He defines maturity, by the way, in a way I have never forgotten: the balance between courage and consideration.
The ability to express your own feelings and convictions with courage, balanced with consideration for the feelings and convictions of others.
High courage with low consideration gets you win-lose.
High consideration with low courage gets you lose-win.
Win-win requires both, at full strength, at the same time, and that is why it is genuinely hard.
Habit five is the one Covey calls the key to all the others, seek first to understand, then to be understood.
He says this is probably the single most important principle in the field of human relations, and it corrects a nearly universal mistake.
When two people communicate, they are usually not listening to understand.
They are listening to reply.
While the other person talks, we are loading our own response, filtering everything through our own experience, our own autobiography.
And so we respond in one of four autobiographical ways.
We evaluate, agreeing or disagreeing.
We probe, asking questions from our own frame of reference.
We advise, giving counsel based on our own experience.
Or we interpret, explaining people's motives based on our own.

Covey gives the example of going to an eye doctor who, after hearing you complain for thirty seconds that you cannot see well, takes off his own glasses and hands them to you, saying, here, wear these, they have worked for me for years.
You put them on and everything is a blur, and he says, just try harder, they work great for me.
That is what we do constantly.
We prescribe before we diagnose.
We hand people our own glasses.
What Covey urges instead is empathic listening, listening with the genuine intent to understand the other person's frame of reference, to see the world as they see it, to feel what they feel.
Not agreeing, necessarily, just understanding.
And he says something profound about why this matters so much.
The deepest need of the human heart is to feel understood.

When a person feels truly understood, when they feel you have really grasped what they are experiencing, the defenses come down, the air clears, and they become open to your influence in a way that was impossible before.
So understanding is not just kind, it is strategic.
Once you have understood, then you seek to be understood, and now you can present your ideas clearly and honestly to a person who is finally ready to hear them.
He lays out five levels of listening, and it is useful to locate yourself honestly on the ladder.
At the bottom is ignoring, not really listening at all.
Above that, pretending, the yeah, uh-huh, right, while your mind is elsewhere.
Above that, selective listening, hearing only certain parts, which is how most of us listen to a chattering four year old.
Above that, attentive listening, paying real attention and focusing energy on the words being said.

And at the top, rare and powerful, empathic listening, listening with the intent to understand, which means getting inside the other person's frame of reference and looking at the world the way they see it.
Only about ten percent of our communication is represented by our words, Covey notes.
Thirty percent is our sounds, and sixty percent is body language.
In empathic listening you listen with your ears, but you also listen with your eyes and with your heart.
You listen for feeling.
You listen for meaning.
You listen for behavior.
His demonstration of this is a father and a teenage son, and it is a masterclass.
The boy says, Dad, I've had it.
School is for the birds.
The reflex answer, the autobiographical answer, is to say, what's wrong, son, or worse, well son, you have to stick it out, education is important, I felt that way too at your age.
Instead, Covey has the father simply reflect the feeling.
You're feeling really frustrated.
And the boy says, yes, it's totally impractical, I'm not getting anything out of it.
And the father says, you feel like school isn't doing you any good.
Right, says the boy, look at Joe, he dropped out, he's fixing cars, he's making money.
Now that's practical.
And so it goes, the father resisting every urge to lecture, just reflecting content and feeling back, until the boy, several exchanges deep, finally says the real thing, quietly: Dad, I'm scared.
I don't think I can read well enough.
If I go on to college, how am I going to read well enough?
That was the actual problem the entire time, and it was buried three layers under a complaint about school being useless.
If the father had answered the first sentence with advice, which is what almost every father in the world would have done, that boy would have walked away and the fear would have stayed buried.
Covey's rule of thumb is a diagnosis before a prescription.
A doctor who prescribes before diagnosing loses their license.
In relationships we do it constantly and call it helping.
Habit six is synergize, and this is the crowning public victory, the habit that produces the miracle of the whole being greater than the sum of its parts.
Synergy is what happens when one plus one equals three, or ten, or a thousand.
It is creative cooperation.
And Covey says the essence of synergy is to value the differences between people, to respect them, to build on strengths and compensate for weaknesses.
The person who is truly effective has the humility to recognize the limits of their own perception and to genuinely appreciate that another person sees things they cannot.
If two people have the same opinion, one of them is unnecessary.

The whole point is that you see it differently than I do, and if we can bring those different views together with trust and open communication, we can arrive at a third alternative, a solution neither of us could have reached alone, better than either of our original ideas.
Most people never experience this because they are stuck defending their own position, trapped in either-or thinking, my way or your way.
Synergy opens a third door.
It requires the emotional bank account to be full, it requires win-win thinking, and it requires the empathic listening of habit five, which is why it comes last.
When those conditions are present, differences stop being obstacles and become the raw material of creation.
Covey gives a small domestic example that makes synergy concrete, and I like it precisely because it is so ordinary.
He wanted to take the family on a boating trip up a lake, a long trip, with plans he had been making for a year.
His wife wanted to visit her ailing mother, three hundred and fifty miles away, and she wanted to be near her during the vacation.
Two positions, apparently incompatible, and the obvious outcomes are that one of them wins and the other quietly resents it, or that they compromise into some half-hearted trip that satisfies nobody.
Instead they talked, really talked, with the empathic listening of habit five and the win-win frame of habit four, until the surface positions dissolved into the underlying interests.
He wanted time together as a family and the adventure he had been anticipating.
She wanted to be a good daughter and not spend the whole holiday feeling guilty.

Once those were on the table, a third alternative appeared that neither had thought of, better than either original plan, and both of them left the conversation genuinely happy rather than half satisfied.
That is the test of synergy.
A compromise leaves one plus one equal to about one and a half.
Synergy leaves it at three, and everyone knows it.
And then, wrapped around all six, comes habit seven, sharpen the saw.
Covey tells the story of a man in the woods sawing furiously at a tree, exhausted, drenched in sweat, and you ask him what he is doing.
He says, I'm sawing down this tree, I've been at it for hours, I'm beat.
You suggest he take a break to sharpen his saw, because that dull blade is why it is taking so long.
And he snaps back, I don't have time to sharpen the saw, I'm too busy sawing.
That, Covey says, is how most of us live.
We are too busy driving to stop for gas.
Sharpening the saw is the habit of self-renewal, of taking time to preserve and enhance the greatest asset you have, which is yourself.
And he says you must renew yourself in four dimensions.
The physical, through exercise, nutrition, and rest.
The mental, through reading, learning, planning, and writing.
The social and emotional, through relationships, service, and connection.
And the spiritual, through meditation, reflection, and time with your deepest values and, for many, their faith.
These four are the leaves of a single plant.
Neglect any one and the others suffer.
And Covey ties this back to a principle he calls production and production capability balance, which he illustrates with the fable of the goose and the golden eggs.
A farmer finds a goose that lays a golden egg every day.
Greedy for more, he kills the goose to get all the eggs at once, and of course finds nothing inside, and now has no more eggs at all.
The eggs are production, the results you want.
The goose is the production capability, the asset that produces the results.
If you focus only on the eggs and neglect the goose, you destroy your ability to produce.
Sharpening the saw is caring for the goose.
It is the daily renewal of the one asset, you, that makes every other habit possible.
So step back and see the whole picture Covey has drawn.
You start on the inside.
Habit one, be proactive, hands you back the power of choice, the recognition that you are responsible, response-able, for your own life.
Habit two, begin with the end in mind, gives that power a direction, a clear vision of what your life is for, anchored in unchanging principles.
Habit three, put first things first, gives you the discipline to live that vision day by day, spending your life in the important quadrant instead of drowning in the merely urgent.
Those three win you the private victory, and make you a genuinely independent person of character.
Then you move outward.
Habit four, think win-win, gives you an abundant, mutual-benefit frame for every relationship.
Habit five, seek first to understand, teaches you to listen your way into another person's world so they can finally hear you.
Habit six, synergize, lets you take your differences and create something together that neither could create alone.
Those three win the public victory and carry you into genuine interdependence, the highest and most productive way of living.
And habit seven, sharpen the saw, renews the whole system, keeping the person who does all of this healthy, sharp, and growing.
The deepest message under all of it is the one Covey started with, sitting in that quiet worry over his struggling son.
Effectiveness is not a set of tricks you apply to other people.
It is not personality, image, or technique.
It is character, built from the inside out, aligned with principles that do not change.
You cannot fake it, and you do not need to, because the real thing is available to anyone willing to work on the person in the mirror first.
Change your paradigms, and you change your behavior.
Change your character, and you change your life.
The way you see the problem, Covey reminds us again and again, is the problem.

And when you learn to see rightly, and to build patiently on true principles, you become not just someone who does effective things, but someone who is, at the core, an effective and whole human being.
There is one more idea Covey saves for the very end, and for a lot of readers it is the part that stays.
He calls it becoming a transition person.
Every one of us inherits scripts.
Tendencies, temperaments, ways of speaking, ways of handling anger or money or affection, passed down through families, sometimes for generations.
Some of that inheritance is a gift.
Some of it is damage, handed forward by people who were themselves handed it, and who mostly did not know they were passing anything on at all.
A transition person is someone who stops the transmission.
Someone who takes the abuse, or the coldness, or the contempt, or the fear that came down the line and simply does not pass it to the next person.
It ends with them.
It is quiet work.
Nobody gives you a medal for the argument you did not have, or the cruelty you absorbed and did not repeat with your own child.
But Covey argues it is among the most powerful things a human being can do with a life, and that every one of the habits is, in a sense, in service of it.
Because being proactive means you are not obligated to repeat what was done to you.
And that, in the end, is the promise of the inside-out approach: that no matter what came before you, the script from here forward is yours to write.
Let me leave you with the practical heart of it, the things you can begin this week.
Catch yourself using reactive language, the I have to and he makes me feel, and deliberately replace it with proactive language, I choose and I will.
Spend an hour writing the first rough draft of your own personal mission statement, starting from that funeral question, what do you want said about you.
Take your calendar and, before the urgent things fill it, schedule the important-but-not-urgent things first, the exercise, the relationship, the planning, the learning.
Make a deliberate deposit in the emotional bank account of someone close to you, a kept promise, an apology, an act of genuine listening.

And in your next real conversation, especially a tense one, stop preparing your reply and instead listen only to understand, reflecting back what the other person feels until they know you truly get it.
Do these, and you will feel the ground shift, because you will have stopped working on the outside and started, at last, from the inside out.
